title: Hurricane Polo's Leftover Rain Floods the Southwest
summary:
Hurricane Polo slammed into Mexico on Tuesday morning with winds of 110 mph (177 kph). By evening, the storm had weakened — but its leftover rain was still causing big problems in the U.S. Southwest.

In New Mexico, flooded roads and debris blocked highways. Hundreds of people in the small towns of Rincon, Salem and Garfield were told to get to higher ground fast. Why? A dam nearby might fail. Later, people in Hatch — a town famous for its green chile crops — and Placitas were told to leave too.

Arizona got soaked. One person was stranded on top of an overturned car west of Phoenix and had to be rescued by a helicopter. In Utah's Zion National Park, a helicopter rescued three people from a canyon after flash flooding.

Desert areas usually get less than 10 inches (25 centimeters) of rain a year, so the ground can't soak up much water. That makes flash floods a constant danger. Meteorologist Carter Greulich warned: "Don't drive through flooded roadways. Remain out of the arroyos."

The flood risk is now moving east — heavy rain is expected in Texas and Oklahoma.
why_it_matters: Knowing how flash floods work can keep your family safe — if you ever see water covering a road, the rule is simple: never drive through it.

background_read: A hurricane is a huge, swirling storm that grows over warm ocean water — it can pack winds of more than 100 miles per hour.
Zion National Park (a protected park in Utah famous for its tall red-rock canyons) is a place where hikers sometimes get trapped when water suddenly rushes through.
Deserts can flood fast because the dry, hard ground cannot soak up rain. That is why flash floods can happen even after the storm itself has moved far away.
Article_Structure: WHO: Hurricane Polo and the people it hit — including families in New Mexico, Arizona and Utah — plus meteorologist Carter Greulich.
WHAT: The hurricane slammed Mexico with 110 mph winds, then its leftover rain flooded roads, forced people to higher ground and stranded drivers.
WHERE: Mexico first, then the U.S. Southwest — New Mexico, Arizona and Utah — with the flood risk now moving east.
WHY: Desert ground cannot soak up much rain, so leftover storm water becomes a dangerous flash flood very quickly.

perspectives.description: Officials told people to leave low areas fast because a dam might fail — protecting lives comes before anything else.
For people in Hatch, a town famous for its green chile crops, the flood water threatens their farms and their income.
Meteorologists say the real danger is not the storm itself but the dry desert ground, which turns rain into rushing water in minutes.
